claims.claim: fever is a regulated rise of the body's temperature set point, orchestrated by the brain — not a loss of temperature control
claims.definition: during fever the hypothalamic set point is elevated and thermoregulatory defenses (vasoconstriction, shivering) operate to defend the higher target, exactly as they defend 37 C at baseline
claims.measured_value: typical fever range 38-40 C core; set-point rise of roughly 1-2 C
claims.authoritative_source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, ch. 74 (thermoregulation and fever); Dinarello & Gelfand, fever chapters in standard internal-medicine references

claims.claim: the hypothalamus, at the base of the brain, acts as the body's thermostat for core temperature
claims.definition: preoptic/anterior hypothalamus integrates thermal signals from skin, viscera and blood and drives heat-production and heat-loss responses
claims.authoritative_source: Guyton & Hall, ch. 74; standard neuroanatomy references

claims.claim: pyrogenic cytokines from immune cells induce prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, which raises the fever set point; antipyretics such as ibuprofen lower fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis (COX)
claims.definition: circulating IL-1/IL-6/TNF act on the brain (humoral and endothelial routes) to induce COX-2-mediated PGE2; PGE2 raises the set point; NSAIDs block COX, lowering PGE2
claims.measured_value: set-point rise commonly ~1-2 C in common infections
claims.authoritative_source: Dinarello, 'Infection, fever and pyrogens' (Ann Rev Physiol); Vane 1971 mechanism of aspirin (Nobel 1982); standard pharmacology references

claims.claim: when the set point rises above core temperature, the body responds as if cold: skin vasoconstriction and shivering generate and retain heat until the new target is met
claims.definition: shivering raises metabolic heat production several-fold; cutaneous vasoconstriction cuts radiant loss; both are set-point-driven
claims.measured_value: shivering can raise metabolic rate roughly 2-5x (studies vary); qualitative direction firm
claims.authoritative_source: Guyton & Hall, ch. 74; cold-stress physiology literature (magnitude ranges vary by study — hedged)

claims.claim: moderate fever can slow replication of many pathogens and support immune function, but very high fevers can be harmful, and how much benefit fever provides in human infections remains debated
claims.definition: in-vitro and animal data show impaired pathogen growth and enhanced immune activity at elevated temperatures; human outcome data are mixed (e.g. antipyretic trial evidence varies by infection) — stated as a hedged trade-off
claims.measured_value: no single number; direction supported, magnitude debated
claims.authoritative_source: Evans et al., 'Fever and the thermal control of bacterial virulence' (mitigation data); Earn et al. on antipyretics and viral evolution; systematic reviews of antipyretic treatment (mixed)

claims.claim: when the set point falls — pyrogens clearing or prostaglandin synthesis blocked — the body is now above target and sheds heat: cutaneous vasodilation and sweating
claims.definition: the same regulated machinery runs in reverse; sweat evaporation dissipates the heat held during the fever ramp
claims.authoritative_source: Guyton & Hall, ch. 74; standard internal-medicine references

claims.claim: normal core temperature is about 36.5-37.5 C and varies between people and across the day, so 37.0 C is an average rather than a fixed law
claims.definition: circadian rhythm of roughly 0.5 C and population variation are well documented; the classic 37 C figure comes from 19th-century averages
claims.measured_value: approx. 36.5-37.5 C normal band; ~0.5 C circadian swing
claims.authoritative_source: normal-body-temperature reviews (e.g. Mackowiak et al. on Wunderlich's legacy); Guyton & Hall
